items.title: Chapter 1: Computer Networks and the Internet
items.text:
• 1.1 What Is the Internet?
  • Nuts-and-bolts vs services view
  • Protocol definition (syntax, semantics, timing)
  • Human protocol analogy
  • 1.2 The Network Edge
  • Access networks: DSL, Cable, FTTH, 5G, Enterprise
  • Physical media: Twisted pair, Coax, Fiber, Radio
  • Dedicated vs shared access
  • 1.3 The Network Core
  • Packet switching vs circuit switching
  • Store-and-forward, statistical multiplexing
  • Network of networks: Tier-1/2/3 ISPs, IXPs, CDNs
  • Peering vs transit
  • 1.4 Delay, Loss, and Throughput
  • Four delay components: processing, queuing, transmission, propagation
  • Caravan analogy (tollbooth)
  • Traffic intensity ρ = La/R, queuing delay formula
  • End-to-end delay, traceroute
  • Bottleneck throughput, M flows sharing
  • 1.5 Protocol Layers
  • 5-layer Internet model vs OSI 7-layer
  • Encapsulation/decapsulation (Matryoshka dolls)
  • 1.6 Networks Under Attack
  • Malware, DoS/DDoS, sniffing, spoofing, MitM, DNS attacks
  • 1.7 History of Computer Networking
  • 1961-1972: ARPANET, NCP
  • 1972-1980: TCP/IP, Ethernet
  • 1980-1990: NSFNET, DNS, congestion control
  • 1990s: Web, commercialization
  • 2000s-present: Broadband, mobile, cloud, SDN, IoT, QUIC

items.title: Chapter 2: Application Layer
items.text:
• 2.1 Principles of Network Applications
  • Client-server vs P2P architectures
  • Processes, sockets (API), addressing (IP + port)
  • Transport services: reliable, throughput, timing, security
  • TCP vs UDP services
  • Application-layer protocol definition
  • 2.2 The Web and HTTP
  • HTTP overview: stateless, URL format
  • Non-persistent vs persistent vs pipelined (RTT calculations)
  • HTTP message format (request/response)
  • Cookies (Set-Cookie, Cookie headers)
  • Browser caching (304 Not Modified)
  • HTTP/2: binary framing, multiplexing, HPACK, server push
  • HTTP/3 over QUIC: 0-RTT, connection migration, no HOL blocking
  • 2.3 Electronic Mail
  • SMTP (push, port 25/587, 7-bit ASCII)
  • Mail formats (RFC 5322, MIME)
  • POP3/IMAP/HTTP for mail access
  • 2.4 DNS
  • Hierarchical distributed DB: root → TLD → authoritative
  • Recursive vs iterative queries
  • Caching with TTL
  • Record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, TXT, SRV
  • DNSSEC, DoH/DoT
  • 2.5 Video Streaming and CDNs
  • Stored, live, interactive video
  • DASH (MPD, adaptive streaming)
  • CDN operation: request routing, content placement, delivery
  • Netflix/YouTube case studies
  • 2.6 Socket Programming
  • UDP: sendto/recvfrom (address included)
  • TCP: connect/accept (welcoming + connection sockets)
  • Python examples for both

items.title: Chapter 3: Transport Layer
items.text:
• 3.1 Introduction and Transport-Layer Services
  • Transport vs network layer (process-to-process vs host-to-host)
  • TCP vs UDP feature comparison
  • 3.2 Multiplexing and Demultiplexing
  • UDP: 2-tuple (dst IP, dst port)
  • TCP: 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port)
  • 3.3 UDP
  • 8-byte header structure
  • Checksum: 1's complement + pseudo-header
  • 3.4 Principles of Reliable Data Transfer
  • rdt 1.0 → 3.0 evolution
  • Stop-and-wait utilization
  • Pipelining: GBN vs SR
  • 3.4.3 Go-Back-N (GBN)
  • Sender/receiver window, cumulative ACK
  • Window bound: N ≤ 2ᵏ - 1
  • Retransmit ALL on timeout
  • Example: 18 transmissions (N=10, every 5th lost)
  • 3.4.4 Selective Repeat (SR)
  • Per-packet timers, individual ACKs
  • Window bound: N ≤ 2ᵏ⁻¹
  • Retransmit only timed-out packet
  • Example: 12 transmissions (same conditions)
  • 3.5 TCP
  • Segment structure: seq/ACK numbers, flags, window, options
  • MSS = MTU - 40
  • RTT estimation (EWMA α=0.125, DevRTT β=0.25)
  • Timeout = EstRTT + 4×DevRTT, Karn's Algorithm
  • Sender events, fast retransmit (3 dup ACKs), fast recovery
  • Flow control (rwnd)
  • 3-way handshake, 4-way teardown, TIME_WAIT
  • 3.6-3.7 Congestion Control
  • Causes/costs of congestion
  • End-end vs network-assisted
  • Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance, Fast Recovery
  • AIMD sawtooth
  • Tahoe, Reno, CUBIC comparison
  • ECN (CE/ECE/CWR bits)
  • Fairness (R/K)
  • 3.8 Evolution
  • TCP (kernel) vs QUIC (user-space)
  • HTTP/3 over QUIC

items.title: Chapter 4: Network Layer - Data Plane
items.text:
• 4.1 Overview
  • Forwarding vs routing
  • Data plane vs control plane
  • Service models (best effort, CBR, ABR, Intserv, Diffserv)
  • 4.2 Router Internals
  • Routing processor (control plane, ms) vs switching fabric (data plane, ns)
  • Input ports: physical → link → lookup (match+action) → queue
  • Longest prefix matching (TCAM)
  • Switching fabrics: memory, bus, crossbar/Clos
  • HOL blocking at input queues
  • Output port queueing, buffer sizing (RTT×C, RTT×C/√N)
  • Buffer management: tail drop, priority, ECN/RED
  • 4.3 IPv4
  • Datagram format (20-byte header)
  • Fragmentation: ID, flags (MF, DF), offset (8-byte units)
  • Why avoid fragmentation
  • 4.4 IPv4 Addressing
  • CIDR (a.b.c.d/x), subnets
  • Hierarchical addressing, route aggregation
  • Classful vs classless
  • ICANN, RIRs, NAT for exhaustion
  • 4.5 NAT
  • Private address spaces (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16)
  • Translation table, outgoing/incoming processing
  • NAT traversal (static port forwarding)

items.title: Chapter 5: Network Layer - Control Plane
items.text:
• 5.1 Routing Algorithms
  • Graph abstraction G=(N,E), c(x,y)
  • Global (Link State) vs Decentralized (Distance Vector)
  • Static vs Dynamic
  • 5.2 Link-State (Dijkstra)
  • Algorithm steps, initialization, loop
  • Example with 6 nodes

  • 5.3 Distance Vector (Bellman-Ford)

items.title: IPv6, ICMP, DHCP
items.text:
• IPv6: 128-bit, 40-byte fixed header, no checksum/fragmentation, flow label, extension headers, address types (unicast/multicast/anycast), transition (tunneling, dual stack)
  • ICMP: Error reporting, ping (Type 8/0), traceroute (Type 11)
  • DHCP: DORA (Discover/Offer/Request/ACK), lease, options (gateway, DNS, mask)

items.title: Chapter 6: Link Layer and LANs
items.text:
• 6.1 Introduction
  • Nodes, links, frames
  • Services: framing, link access, MAC addressing, reliable delivery, error detection/correction, flow control, half/full duplex
  • Implementation: NIC/on-chip
  • 6.2 Error Detection and Correction
  • Single-bit parity (even), 2D parity (detect+correct)
  • Internet checksum (1's complement)
  • CRC (polynomial division, D×2ʳ mod G)
  • 6.3 Multiple Access Protocols
  • Channel partitioning (TDMA/FDMA/CDMA)
  • Random access (CSMA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA)
  • Taking turns (polling, token)
  • CSMA/CD: listen before transmit, binary exponential backoff
  • CSMA/CA: DIFS, backoff, ACK, RTS/CTS
  • Modern Ethernet: no collision detection
  • 6.4 Switched LANs
  • MAC addresses (48-bit, flat, portable) vs IP (32-bit, hierarchical)
  • Private WiFi addresses
  • ARP: broadcast query → unicast reply, ARP table with TTL
  • Routing to another subnet (IP end-to-end, MAC per-hop)
  • 6.5 Ethernet
  • Bus vs switched topology
  • Frame structure (preamble, addresses, type, data, CRC)
  • Min 64B, max 1518B
  • Unreliable, connectionless
  • 6.6 Ethernet Switches
  • Self-learning (src MAC → port), flooding, forwarding
  • Interconnecting switches
  • Switches vs routers (L2 vs L3)
  • Broadcast domain, VLANs
  • 6.7 VLANs
  • 802.1Q tag (4 bytes: TPID, priority, DEI, VLAN ID 12b)
  • Access vs trunk ports, native VLAN
  • VLAN-aware forwarding, inter-VLAN routing
  • 6.8 A Day in the Life
  • DHCP → ARP → DNS → TCP handshake → HTTP → Link layer
  • 6.9 Physical Layer
  • Encoding: NRZ, Manchester, 4B/5B, 8B/10B
  • Media: twisted pair, coax, fiber, wireless
  • 6.10 Wireless LANs (802.11)
  • BSS/ESS, channels, association
  • Standards evolution (b/g/n/ac/ax/be)
  • CSMA/CA, RTS/CTS, hidden/exposed terminal
  • Power management

items.title: 3.1 UDP Checksum (Internet Checksum)
items.text:
Sender (1's complement): 

1. Sum all 16-bit words (header + data + pseudo-header)
2. Add wrap-around carry to LSB
3. Checksum = ~Sum (flip all bits)

Receiver: 

Total = Sum(all 16-bit words) + Checksum
If Total == 0xFFFF → No error
Else → Error detected

Pseudo-header: SrcIP(32) | DstIP(32) | Zero(8) | Protocol(8) | Length(16)

items.title: Stop-and-Wait
items.text:
U = (L/R) / (RTT + L/R)
Throughput = L / (RTT + L/R)

items.title: Pipelined (Window N)
items.text:
U = min(1, N × (L/R) / (RTT + L/R))
N_optimal = 1 + (RTT × R) / L
BDP = R × RTT
Packets_in_flight = (R × RTT) / L

items.title: 3.3 Go-Back-N (GBN)
items.text:
Constraint Formula Window Bound N ≤ 2ᵏ - 1 (k = seq num bits) Sender Window base = oldest unACKed, nextseqnum = next to send On Timeout Retransmit ALL packets [base, nextseqnum-1] Utilization U = N × (L/R) / (RTT + L/R) (if N < N_optimal)

18-Transmission Problem (N=10, every 5th lost): - Round 1: 10 tx, Round 2: 6 tx, Round 3: 2 tx = 18 total

items.title: 3.4 Selective Repeat (SR)
items.text:
Constraint Formula Window Bound N ≤ 2ᵏ⁻¹ (Proof: 2N ≤ 2ᵏ → N ≤ 2ᵏ⁻¹) Sender Window [base, base+N-1], per-packet timers On Timeout(n) Retransmit only packet n Receiver Buffers out-of-order in [rcv_base, rcv_base+N-1] Utilization Same as GBN but fewer retransmissions

12-Transmission Problem (same conditions): - Round 1: 10 tx, Round 2: 2 tx = 12 total

items.text: Concept Formula Sequence Number Byte number of FIRST data byte in segment Acknowledgment Number Next expected byte (cumulative) MSS MSS = MTU - 40 (typical: 1500 - 40 = 1460 bytes)

items.title: 3.9 TCP Connection Management
items.text: Phase Packets 3-Way Handshake SYN(x) → SYN+ACK(y, x+1) → ACK(x+1, y+1) 4-Way Teardown FIN(x) → ACK(x+1) → FIN(y) → ACK(y+1) TIME_WAIT 2 × MSL ≈ 2 minutes (MSL ≈ 60s)

items.title: State Variables
items.text:
• cwnd = congestion window (sender limit)
  • ssthresh = slow start threshold
  • EffectiveWindow = min(cwnd, rwnd)

items.title: Slow Start
items.text:
cwnd = 1 MSS (up to 10 MSS per RFC 3390)
Per ACK: cwnd += 1 MSS  (doubles per RTT)
Exit: cwnd ≥ ssthresh → Congestion Avoidance

items.title: Congestion Avoidance
items.text:
Per RTT: cwnd += 1 MSS (linear)
Per ACK: cwnd += MSS × (MSS / cwnd)

items.title: Loss Reactions
items.text: Event Action Timeout ssthresh = cwnd/2; cwnd = 1 MSS; Slow Start 3 Dup ACKs ssthresh = cwnd/2; cwnd = ssthresh + 3 MSS; Fast Recovery

items.title: Fast Recovery
items.text:
On each dup ACK: cwnd += 1 MSS
On new ACK: cwnd = ssthresh; exit to Congestion Avoidance

items.title: Unit 1: Computer Networks and the Internet (Chapter 1)
A Nuts-and-Bolts Description
items.text:
The Internet is a global network of networks - a complex infrastructure consisting of: - End systems (hosts): Computers, smartphones, servers, IoT devices (19 billion devices in 2025, 29 billion by 2030) - Communication links: Fiber optics, copper wire, coaxial cable, radio spectrum, satellite links - Packet switches: Routers and link-layer switches that forward packets - Protocols: TCP, IP, HTTP, DNS, etc. that control communication

Key concept: The Internet provides a service model to applications - a set of operations (send/receive) and expected behavior (reliability, timing, etc.)

items.title: A Services Description
items.text:
The Internet provides two key services to applications: 1. Connectionless service (UDP): Unreliable, no handshake, minimal overhead 2. Connection-oriented service (TCP): Reliable, in-order byte stream with flow/congestion control

Applications access these services via sockets - the API between application and transport layer. The socket interface is the "door" through which applications send/receive messages.

items.title: What Is a Protocol?
items.text:
A protocol defines the format, order, and actions taken on transmission/receipt of messages among communicating entities. - Syntax: Message format, data representation - Semantics: Meaning of fields, actions to take - Timing: When to send, how fast, timeouts

Example: HTTP defines how a client requests a web page and how a server responds.

Human analogy: "Hi" → "Hi" → "What's the time?" → "2:00" - specific messages sent, specific actions taken on receipt.

items.title: 1.2.1 Access Networks
items.text:
Access networks connect end systems to the first router (edge router). Types:

Access Network Technology Typical Speed Characteristics DSL Digital Subscriber Line ~24 Mbps downstream (up to 1 Gbps latest standard) Uses existing telephone lines; dedicated per household; asymmetric (downstream > upstream); distance limited to ~5-10 miles from CO Cable HFC (Hybrid Fiber-Coax) ~1-2 Gbps downstream (DOCSIS 3.0: 1.2 Gbps) Shared broadcast medium; uses DOCSIS; asymmetric; collision possible on upstream FTTH Fiber to the Home ~1-10 Gbps Dedicated fiber; highest speeds; PON (passive optical network) common 5G/Fixed Wireless Cellular ~100 Mbps - 1 Gbps Mobile/wireless; shared spectrum; beam-forming Enterprise (Ethernet/WiFi) 802.3/802.11 ~1-100 Gbps Wired/wireless LAN in organizations LEO Satellites Low Earth Orbit ~100 Mbps Rural/remote; ~10ms latency (vs 280ms GEO)

Key distinction: - Dedicated access (DSL, FTTH): Bandwidth not shared - Shared access (Cable, WiFi, 5G): Bandwidth shared among users

DSL detail: Uses telephone line with frequency-division multiplexing: high-speed downstream (50 kHz-1 MHz), medium-speed upstream (4-50 kHz), telephone (0-4 kHz). DSLAM at central office.

Cable detail: HFC = fiber to neighborhood junctions, coax to homes. CMTS at head end. Shared broadcast medium - all packets travel to all homes.

FTTH detail: PON architecture - OLT at CO, splitter combines <100 homes on shared fiber, ONT at home.

items.text: Medium Type Characteristics Twisted Pair (Cat 5e/6/6a/7) Copper 100m max; 1-10 Gbps; susceptible to interference; dominant for LANs Coaxial Cable Copper Longer distances; used in cable TV/HFC; shared medium; concentric conductors Fiber Optics (SMF/MMF) Glass Km distances; 10-100+ Gbps; immune to EMI; low attenuation; preferred for long-haul Radio Spectrum Wireless WiFi, 4G/5G, satellite; shared medium; variable propagation Terrestrial Radio Wireless Short (1-2m), local (10-100s m), wide-area (10s km) Satellite Radio Wireless GEO: 36,000km, 280ms RTT; LEO: much lower latency

items.title: 1.3.1 Packet Switching
items.text:
The Internet uses packet switching (not circuit switching): - Messages broken into packets (typically 1-1500 bytes) - Each packet routed independently through network - Store-and-forward: Each switch receives entire packet before forwarding to next link - Statistical multiplexing: Links shared on demand; no reservation

Store-and-forward delay: For N links of rate R, single packet delay = N × L/R For P packets back-to-back: delay = (N + P - 1) × L/R

Example: 3 packets, 2 links (1 router). At t=0 send pkt1. At t=L/R router begins forwarding pkt1, source sends pkt2. At t=2L/R dest receives pkt1, router receives pkt2. At t=3L/R dest receives pkt2, router receives pkt3. At t=4L/R all 3 received.

Advantages over Circuit Switching: - Efficient for bursty data traffic (statistical multiplexing) - No connection setup delay - Better resource utilization - Robust (packets can take different paths)

Statistical Multiplexing Example: 1 Gbps link, 1 Mbps/user, 10% active. Circuit: 1000 users max. Packet: ~5000+ users (statistically, low blocking).

items.title: 1.3.2 Circuit Switching (for comparison)
items.text:
• Dedicated end-to-end path reserved for duration of connection
  • Constant bandwidth guaranteed (FDM or TDM)
  • Used in traditional telephone networks
  • Inefficient for bursty traffic (resources idle during silence)
  • FDM: Frequency bands (e.g., 4 kHz per call)
  • TDM: Time slots in frames (e.g., 8000 frames/sec × 8 bits = 64 kbps per circuit)

items.title: 1.3.3 A Network of Networks
items.text:
The Internet = Interconnected ISPs:

Network Structure Evolution: 1. Structure 1: Single global transit ISP (customer-provider) 2. Structure 2: Multiple global transit ISPs (must interconnect) 3. Structure 3: Regional ISPs added (multi-tier hierarchy) 4. Structure 4: PoPs, multi-homing, peering, IXPs 5. Structure 5: Content provider networks (Google, Netflix, etc.)

Tiered ISPs: 1. Tier-1 ISPs: Global reach, peer with each other settlement-free (AT&T, NTT, Tata, Level 3) 2. Tier-2/Regional ISPs: Regional, buy transit from Tier-1 3. Tier-3/Access ISPs: Local, connect end users

Peering vs Transit: - Peering: Mutual agreement, no payment (typically Tier-1 to Tier-1, or same-level ISPs) - Transit: Customer pays provider for global connectivity

IXPs: Internet Exchange Points - physical locations where ISPs peer (NIXI: 77 nodes in India, >1.5 Tbps peak)

Content Providers: Google, Netflix, Akamai, Cloudflare - deploy private networks, peer at IXPs, bypass tier-1 when possible

items.title: 1.4 Delay, Loss, and Throughput in Packet-Switched Networks
1.4.1 Overview of Delay in Packet-Switched Networks
items.text:
Total nodal delay at each router: 

d_nodal = d_proc + d_queue + d_trans + d_prop

Delay Component Formula Description Processing Delay (d_proc) ~microseconds Header check, routing table lookup, bit-error check Queuing Delay (d_queue) Variable Time waiting in output buffer; depends on traffic intensity Transmission Delay (d_trans) L / R Time to push packet bits onto link Propagation Delay (d_prop) d / s Time for bits to travel across link (speed of light ~2×10⁸ m/s in fiber)

Transmission Delay: d_trans = L / R - L = packet length (bits) - R = link bandwidth (bps)

Propagation Delay: d_prop = d / s - d = link length (meters) - s = propagation speed (m/s)

Transmission vs Propagation: - Transmission: function of packet length & link rate, NOT distance - Propagation: function of distance, NOT packet length or rate

items.title: 1.4.2 Caravan Analogy (Tollbooth)
items.text:
• Cars = bits, Caravan = packet, Tollbooth = router
  • Transmission delay = time to push entire caravan through tollbooth (10 cars × 12 sec = 120 sec)
  • Propagation delay = time for car to travel between tollbooths (100 km / 100 km/hr = 1 hr)
  • Total = transmission + propagation = 62 minutes

Key insight: If transmission delay > propagation delay, first cars arrive at next tollbooth before last cars leave first tollbooth. Same in networks - first bits arrive at next router while remaining bits still being transmitted.

items.title: 1.4.3 Numerical Examples (Which Delay Wins?)
items.text:
Scenario A: 5 MB image, 1 Gbps fiber, 12,000 km away - d_prop = 12,000,000 / (2×10⁸) = 60 ms - d_trans = (5×10⁶×8) / 10⁹ = 40 ms - Propagation dominates

Scenario B: 5 MB image, 1 Mbps dial-up, next door - d_prop ≈ negligible - d_trans = (5×10⁶×8) / 10⁶ = 40 seconds - Transmission dominates

items.title: 1.4.4 Queuing Delay and Packet Loss
items.text:
Traffic Intensity: ρ = (L × a) / R = λL / R - a = average packet arrival rate (packets/sec) - λ = a (arrival rate) - ρ = fraction of time link is busy

Traffic Intensity Behavior ρ < 1 Stable, finite average queue ρ → 1 Queue grows, delay increases dramatically ρ > 1 Unstable, queue → ∞, packets dropped

Average Queuing Delay (M/M/1 queue): 

d_queue = (L/R) × (ρ / (1-ρ))

Congestion Multiplier: ρ/(1-ρ) - ρ=0.5 → 1× (delay = 1 transmission time) - ρ=0.8 → 4× - ρ=0.9 → 9× - ρ=0.99 → 99×

Packet Loss: Occurs when buffer is full (finite capacity). Lost packets may be retransmitted (TCP) or lost forever (UDP).

Numerical Example: R=10 Mbps, L=1000 bits → d_trans=100 μs. At a=1000 pkt/s, I=0.1 → d_queue≈11.1 μs. Raise to a=9000 (I=0.9) → d_queue=900 μs (9× arrivals → 81× delay).

items.title: 1.4.5 End-to-End Delay
items.text:
For N links (no queuing/processing): 

d_end-end = N × (d_trans + d_prop)

General case: 

d_end-end = Σ(d_proc_i + d_queue_i + d_trans_i + d_prop_i)

Traceroute: Measures RTT to each router by sending packets with TTL=1,2,3... Router with TTL=0 sends ICMP Time Exceeded. Three probes per hop.

items.title: 1.4.6 Throughput in Computer Networks
items.text:
Instantaneous Throughput: Rate at which receiver gets bits Average Throughput: F / T (file size / transfer time)

Bottleneck Link: The link with minimum rate along path 

Throughput = min(R₁, R₂, ..., R_N)  (no cross traffic)

M flows sharing bottleneck R: 

Throughput_per_flow = R / M

Interactive Exercise Example: - 4 servers, 4 clients, 4 three-hop paths sharing middle link R=300 Mbps - RS=50 Mbps (server links), RC=90 Mbps (client links) - Per-connection throughput = min(50, 90, 300/4) = 50 Mbps - Bottleneck = Rs (50 Mbps) - Server utilization = 50/50 = 1.0 - Client utilization = 50/90 = 0.56 - Shared link utilization = 50/(300/4) = 0.67

items.title: 1.5 Protocol Layers and Their Service Models
1.5.1 Layered Architecture
items.text:
Five-Layer Internet Model: | Layer | Name | Key Protocols | Responsibility | |-------|------|---------------|----------------| | 5 | Application | HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP | Network applications | | 4 | Transport | TCP, UDP | Process-to-process delivery | | 3 | Network | IP, ICMP, routing protocols | Host-to-host delivery, routing | | 2 | Link | Ethernet, WiFi, PPP | Node-to-node delivery | | 1 | Physical | Cables, radio waves | Bit transmission |

OSI 7-Layer Model (for reference): 7. Application, 6. Presentation, 5. Session, 4. Transport, 3. Network, 2. Data Link, 1. Physical - Internet stack "missing" presentation & session - implemented in application if needed

Why Layering?: - Explicit structure for complex systems - Modularization eases maintenance/updating - Change in layer implementation transparent to rest of system

items.title: 1.5.2 Encapsulation
items.text:
Each layer adds its own header (and sometimes trailer): 

Application Message (M)
    → Transport Header (Ht) + M = Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP)
        → IP Header (Hn) + Segment = Datagram
            → Link Header (Hl) + Datagram + Link Trailer = Frame
                → Physical layer transmits bits

Matryoshka Dolls Analogy: Nested encapsulation like stacking dolls.

At each router: Decapsulate to link layer, process IP header, re-encapsulate in new frame. - Link-layer switch: layers 1-2 only - Router: layers 1-3 - Host: all 5 layers

items.title: 1.6 Networks Under Attack
items.text:
Types of attacks: 1. Malware: Viruses, worms, botnets, ransomware (self-replicating, spreads exponentially) 2. DoS/DDoS: Overwhelm target with traffic (vulnerability attack, bandwidth flooding, connection flooding) 3. Sniffing/Eavesdropping: Passive interception (wireless, cable, Ethernet broadcast) 4. Spoofing: Fake source IP/email (IP spoofing) 5. Man-in-the-Middle: Intercept and modify 6. DNS Attacks: Cache poisoning, hijacking

Defense: Firewalls, IDS/IPS, encryption (TLS/IPsec), authentication, access control

items.title: 1.7 History of Computer Networking
items.text:
Era Key Developments 1961-1972 Packet switching theory (Kleinrock 1961, Baran 1964, Davies); ARPANET (1969, 4 nodes); NCP protocol; first email (Tomlinson 1972) 1972-1980 TCP/IP (Cerf & Kahn 1974); Ethernet (Metcalfe 1976); ALOHAnet; separation of TCP/IP/UDP 1980-1990 TCP/IP standardized (1983); DNS (1984); NSFNET backbone (56kbps→1.5Mbps); congestion control (Jacobson 1988) 1990s Web (Berners-Lee 1989-91); Mosaic/Netscape; Commercial ISPs; Dot-com boom; 4 killer apps: email, Web, IM, P2P (Napster) 2000s-Present Broadband, WiFi, Mobile (3G/4G/5G), Cloud, CDNs, SDN, IoT, QUIC/HTTP/3, generative AI

Key Milestones: - 1969: First ARPANET packet (UCLA→SRI, "Lo" before crash) - 1983: TCP/IP flag day (NCP→TCP/IP) - 1991: NSFNET allows commercial use - 2011: Wireless devices > wired devices

Q1. One-hop transmission delay: Given L=8000 bits, R=1 Mbps, calculate d_trans and max packets/sec. - Answer: d_trans = 8 ms, max packets/sec = R/L = 125

Q2. Queuing delay: R=1,900,000 bps, L=4700 bits - a) a=35: I=0.0865 → d_queue=0.23 ms - b) a=77: I=0.19 → d_queue=0.58 ms - c) 613 packets arrive, infinite buffer: fill rate = 613 - R/L = 209 pkts/sec - d) Buffer=627: packets dropped = 613 - (404 + 209) = 0

Q3. End-to-end delay (3 links): L=12000 bits, links: 100Mbps/3km, 1Mbps/5000km, 10Mbps/1km - Link 1: d_trans=0.12ms, d_prop=0.01ms, total=0.13ms - Link 2: d_trans=12ms, d_prop=16.67ms, total=28.67ms - Link 3: d_trans=1.2ms, d_prop=0.003ms, total=1.203ms - Total = 30ms

Q5. Store-and-forward timing: N=3 links, L=12000 bits, R=100 Mbps. How long for 1 packet? For 3 packets back-to-back? - 1 packet: 3 × 12000/100000000 = 0.36 ms - 3 packets: (3+3-1) × 12000/100000000 = 0.6 ms

  17. Cars=bits, caravan=packet, tollbooth=router. Transmission=pushing caravan through tollbooth. Propagation=driving between tollbooths.

  18. How does traceroute work?

  19. Sends packets with TTL=1,2,3... Router with TTL=0 sends ICMP Time Exceeded. Measures RTT.

  20. What are the 5 layers of the Internet stack?

    • Physical, Link, Network, Transport, Application

items.title: Multiple Choice Questions (from Slides)
items.text:
Q1. Shared or private? For each link, decide whether other nodes compete for the same channel. - Your laptop's cable to a switch port → Private (one at each end) - The Wi-Fi in this classroom → Shared (one radio channel) - Cable-TV internet, homes sending upstream → Shared (one cable) - Your phone to a cell tower → Shared (the tower schedules)

Q2. An ideal Multiple access protocol desiderata: 1. When one node wants to transmit, it can send at rate R 2. When M nodes want to transmit, each can send at average rate R/M 3. Fully decentralized: no special node to coordinate, no synchronization of clocks/slots 4. Simple

Q3. Which statement about Ethernet CSMA/CD is TRUE? - a) Collisions detected within long time → False (short time) - b) Colliding transmissions aborted, reducing channel wastage → True - c) Collision detection easy with wireless → False (easy in wired, difficult in wireless) - d) After n collisions, NIC chooses K from {0,1,2,..., 2m} → False ({0,1,2,..., 2m-1})

Q4. Is collision detection still used? - Modern switched Ethernet: No (full-duplex, separate channels) - Wi-Fi: Still shared, collisions happen

items.title: 2.1.1 Network Application Architectures
items.text:
Two main paradigms:

Architecture Description Examples Client-Server Always-on server (fixed IP) serves clients; clients don't communicate directly; often data centers for scaling Web, Email, DNS, Video Streaming Peer-to-Peer (P2P) No always-on server; peers act as both clients and servers; self-scaling (new peers bring capacity + demand) BitTorrent, Bitcoin, Skype (original)

Hybrid: Many modern apps use both (e.g., P2P for content, centralized for discovery/auth).

Key Insight: Application architecture ≠ Network architecture. Network architecture (5-layer stack) is fixed; application architecture is chosen by developer.

items.title: 2.1.2 Processes Communicating
items.text:
• Process: Program running within a host (not the program itself, but its execution instance)
  • Client process: Initiates communication
  • Server process: Waits to be contacted
  • Inter-process communication: Same host (OS-defined); Different hosts (exchange messages over network)

items.title: 2.1.3 Sockets
items.text:
• Socket: Interface between application process and transport-layer protocol
  • Analogy: Process = house, Socket = door
  • Sending process shoves message out its door (socket)
  • Transport infrastructure on other side delivers to receiving process's door
  • Application developer controls: Application-layer side of socket
  • OS controls: Transport-layer side of socket
  • Developer choices: (1) Transport protocol (TCP/UDP), (2) Few parameters (buffer sizes, MSS)

items.title: 2.1.4 Addressing Processes
items.text: To receive messages, process needs identifier: - Host identifier: 32-bit IP address - Process identifier: Port number (16-bit) - Example: Web server: IP + port 80; Mail server: IP + port 25

items.title: 2.1.5 Transport Services Available to Applications
items.text:
Four dimensions:

Service Description Reliable Data Transfer Guaranteed delivery without errors, in order (TCP) vs loss-tolerant (UDP) Throughput Guaranteed minimum rate (not provided by Internet) vs elastic (use whatever) Timing Guaranteed max delay (not provided) vs best-effort Security Encryption, integrity, authentication (TLS enhances TCP)

Services NOT provided by Internet transport protocols: Throughput guarantees, Timing guarantees

items.title: 2.1.6 Transport Services Provided by the Internet
items.text:
Feature TCP UDP Connection Connection-oriented (3-way handshake) Connectionless Reliability Reliable, in-order byte stream Unreliable, may arrive out of order Flow Control Yes (receiver buffer) No Congestion Control Yes (throttles sender) No Security Via TLS (application layer) Via DTLS Header Overhead 20+ bytes 8 bytes

Application Protocol Mapping: - TCP: HTTP, SMTP, FTP, SSH, IMAP - UDP: DNS, RTP, DHCP, SIP, QUIC - Either: Video conferencing (UDP preferred, TCP fallback for firewalls)

items.title: 2.1.7 Application-Layer Protocols
items.text:
Define: - Message types (request/response) - Message syntax (fields, delineation) - Field semantics (meaning) - Rules for when/how to send/respond

Open protocols (RFCs): HTTP, SMTP, DNS - interoperability Proprietary protocols: Zoom, Skype (original)

items.title: 2.2.1 Overview of HTTP
items.text:
• HTTP: HyperText Transfer Protocol (RFC 1945, 7230, 7540, 9114)
  • Client: Browser (requests, receives, displays objects)
  • Server: Web server (sends objects in response)
  • Objects: HTML, JPEG, JavaScript, CSS, video - each addressable by URL
  • Web page: Base HTML + referenced objects (e.g., HTML + 5 images = 6 objects)
  • URL format: http://hostname/path (hostname + path name)
  • Stateless: Server maintains no client state between requests

items.title: 2.2.2 Non-Persistent vs Persistent Connections
items.text:
Connection Type Description RTTs for K objects Non-persistent (HTTP/1.0) New TCP connection per object K × 2 RTTs Persistent (HTTP/1.1) Single TCP connection for multiple objects 2 RTT + K×trans Pipelined Persistent Send requests back-to-back without waiting 2 RTT + K×trans

HTTP/1.0: Default non-persistent (can use Connection: keep-alive) HTTP/1.1: Default persistent, supports pipelining (rarely used due to HOL blocking)

Numerical Example: 1 HTML + 6 images, RTT=80ms, transmission negligible - Non-persistent: 7 × 2 × 80 = 1120 ms - Persistent (no pipelining): 1 (TCP) + 7 (req/resp) = 8 RTT = 640 ms - Persistent (pipelining): 1 (TCP) + 1 (HTML) + 1 (all images) = 3 RTT = 240 ms

items.title: 2.2.3 HTTP Message Format
items.text:
Request Message: 

GET /somedir/page.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.someschool.edu
Connection: close
User-agent: Mozilla/5.0
Accept-language: fr

[empty line]
[entity body - empty for GET, form data for POST]

Components: - Request line: Method (GET, POST, HEAD, PUT, DELETE), URL, HTTP version - Header lines: Host, Connection, User-agent, Accept-language, etc. - Entity body: For POST (form data), PUT (file upload)

Response Message: 

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Connection: close
Date: Mon, 21 Oct 2024 18:58:21 GMT
Server: Apache/2.2.3
Last-Modified: Sun, 20 Oct 2024 13:20:46 GMT
Content-Length: 6821
Content-Type: text/html

<html>...</html>

Components: - Status line: Version, status code, phrase - Header lines: Date, Server, Last-Modified, Content-Length, Content-Type - Entity body: Requested object

Common Methods: GET (retrieve), POST (submit form), HEAD (headers only), PUT (upload), DELETE (remove)

Common Status Codes: - 200 OK, 301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified - 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found - 505 HTTP Version Not Supported

items.title: 2.2.4 User-Server Interaction: Cookies
items.text:
Problem: HTTP is stateless; servers need to identify users across requests Solution: Cookies (RFC 6265)

Four Components: 1. Set-cookie header in HTTP response 2. Cookie header in subsequent HTTP requests 3. Cookie file on user's host (managed by browser) 4. Back-end database at Web site

How it works: 1. User visits site first time → Server creates unique ID, stores in database 2. Server responds with Set-cookie: 1678 3. Browser stores hostname, 1678 in cookie file 4. Subsequent requests include Cookie: 1678 5. Server tracks user activity, enables shopping cart, recommendations

Privacy: Third-party cookies (ad networks) track across sites; restricted by modern browsers

items.title: 2.2.5 Browser Caching
items.text:
Goal: Reduce latency, bandwidth, server load Mechanism: - Server sends Cache-Control: max-age=3600 or Expires - Browser caches response - Conditional GET: If stale, send If-Modified-Since: <date> - Server responds 304 Not Modified (no object) if unchanged - 304 saves bandwidth and response time

Cache-Control directives: no-store, max-age, must-revalidate, etc.

items.title: 2.2.6 HTTP/2 (RFC 7540)
items.text:
Goals: Reduce latency, eliminate HOL blocking, header compression Key Features: 1. Binary framing (not text) - efficient parsing 2. Multiplexing - multiple streams over single TCP connection 3. Header compression (HPACK) - reduces overhead 4. Server push - send resources proactively 5. Stream prioritization - critical resources first

HOL Blocking Problem in HTTP/1.1: Single TCP connection → large object blocks small ones behind it HTTP/2 Solution: Frame interleaving - break messages into frames, interleave on same connection

Example: Video (1000 frames) + 8 small objects (2 frames each) - With interleaving: Small objects sent after 18 frames - Without: Small objects wait for 1016 frames

Limitation: HOL blocking still at TCP level (lost packet blocks all streams)

items.title: 2.2.7 HTTP/3 and QUIC (RFC 9114, RFC 9000)
items.text:
QUIC: Quick UDP Internet Connections - Runs over UDP (not TCP) - Implements reliability, congestion control, TLS 1.3 in user space - 0-RTT resumption for repeat connections - Connection migration - survives IP change (mobile handoff) - Per-stream flow control - no HOL blocking across streams

HTTP/3 = HTTP semantics over QUIC

Handshake Comparison: - TCP + TLS 1.2: 2 RTT - TCP + TLS 1.3: 1 RTT - QUIC + TLS 1.3: 1 RTT - QUIC 0-RTT: 0 RTT (resumption)

items.title: 2.3.1 SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol)
items.text:
• Port 25 (server-to-server), Port 587 (client submission with TLS)
  • Push protocol: Sender pushes to receiver
  • Text-based commands: HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, QUIT
  • Reliable: Uses TCP
  • 7-bit ASCII only (requires MIME for binary/attachments)

Flow: 

Client → MTA → ... → MTA → Recipient's Mail Server

items.title: 2.3.2 Mail Message Formats
items.text:
RFC 5322 (message format): 

From: sender@example.com
To: recipient@example.com
Subject: Hello
Date: Mon, 03 Nov 2026 12:00:00 GMT
Message-ID: <unique@id>

Body text here...

MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) - RFC 2045: - Content-Type: text/plain, text/html, multipart/mixed, image/jpeg, etc. - Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64, quoted-printable, 7bit - Enables attachments, non-ASCII, multipart messages

items.title: 2.3.3 Mail Access Protocols
items.text:
Protocol Port Description POP3 110 (995 TLS) Download and delete; simple, offline access IMAP 143 (993 TLS) Remote folder management; sync across devices; server-side search HTTP 80/443 Webmail (Gmail, Outlook.com) - uses web API

SMTP = sending mail; POP3/IMAP = reading mail

items.title: 2.4.1 Services Provided by DNS
items.text:
1. Hostname to IP translation (primary)
  2. Host aliasing (CNAME records)
  3. Mail server aliasing (MX records)
  4. Load distribution (multiple A records for same name)
  5. Service discovery (SRV records)

items.title: 2.4.2 Overview of How DNS Works
items.text:
Hierarchical, distributed database: 

Root (.) → TLD (.com, .org, .edu) → Authoritative (example.com)

DNS Servers: 1. Root servers (13 logical, hundreds physical): Know TLD servers 2. TLD servers: Know authoritative servers for domains 3. Authoritative servers: Know actual records for domain 4. Local/Recursive resolvers: ISP/company DNS; perform recursive queries

Query Types: - Recursive: Resolver does all work, returns final answer - Iterative: Resolver asks root → TLD → authoritative step by step

Caching: All responses cached (TTL typically 2 days = 172,800 sec)

Messages for 3-level lookup: 8 messages (4 queries + 4 replies)

items.title: 2.4.3 DNS Records and Messages
items.text:
Resource Record Format: (Name, Value, Type, TTL)

Type Name Value Purpose A hostname IPv4 address Name → IPv4 AAAA hostname IPv6 address Name → IPv6 CNAME alias canonical name Alias → real name MX domain mail server hostname Mail routing NS domain authoritative NS Delegation TXT domain arbitrary text SPF, DKIM, verification SRV service host:port Service discovery

DNS Message Format: 

Header (12 bytes): ID, flags, QDCOUNT, ANCOUNT, NSCOUNT, ARCOUNT
Question Section: QNAME, QTYPE, QCLASS
Answer Section: RRs
Authority Section: RRs
Additional Section: RRs

Flags: QR (0=query, 1=response), Opcode, AA (authoritative), TC (truncated), RD (recursion desired), RA (recursion available), RCODE

items.title: 2.4.4 DNS Security
items.text:
• DNSSEC: Cryptographic signatures on records (RRSIG, DNSKEY, DS)
  • DoH/DoT: DNS over HTTPS/TLS for privacy
  • Attacks: Cache poisoning, DDoS on root/TLD, hijacking

items.title: 2.5 Video Streaming and Content Distribution Networks
2.5.1 Internet Video
items.text: Characteristics: High bandwidth, delay-tolerant (buffering), loss-tolerant Types: - Stored video: YouTube, Netflix (pre-recorded) - Live streaming: Twitch, sports (real-time encoding) - Interactive video: Zoom, FaceTime (low latency critical)

items.title: 2.5.2 HTTP Streaming and DASH
items.text:
Problem: Traditional streaming (RTSP/RTP) doesn't traverse firewalls well Solution: DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) - Video encoded at multiple bitrates/qualities - MPD (Media Presentation Description): XML manifest listing segments - Client adapts quality based on measured bandwidth - Segments fetched via standard HTTP GET

Quality adaptation algorithms: Buffer-based, throughput-based, hybrid

items.title: 2.5.3 Content Distribution Networks (CDNs)
items.text:
Problem: Single server far from users → high latency, low throughput CDN Solution: Deploy server clusters (PoPs) globally

CDN Operations: 1. Request routing: DNS redirects to nearest PoP (GeoDNS, anycast) 2. Content placement: Popular content cached at edge 3. Content delivery: Serve from cache or fetch from origin

Types: - Private CDNs: Netflix Open Connect, Google Global Cache - Third-party CDNs: Akamai, Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront

Benefits: Lower latency, higher throughput, reduced origin load, DDoS absorption

Netflix Case Study: - Open Connect Appliances deployed at ISPs - Pre-positions content based on viewing predictions - ~15% of global Internet traffic

items.title: 2.6.1 Socket Programming with UDP
items.text:
UDP Socket API (Python): 

# Server
serverSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM)
serverSocket.bind(('', port))
while True:
    message, clientAddress = serverSocket.recvfrom(2048)
    serverSocket.sendto(modifiedMessage, clientAddress)

# Client
clientSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM)
clientSocket.sendto(message, (serverName, serverPort))
modifiedMessage, serverAddress = clientSocket.recvfrom(2048)

Key points: - sendto()/recvfrom() include destination address - No connection setup - Unreliable, unordered

items.title: 2.6.2 Socket Programming with TCP
items.text:
TCP Socket API (Python): 

# Server
serverSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)
serverSocket.bind(('', port))
serverSocket.listen(1)
while True:
    connectionSocket, addr = serverSocket.accept()
    message = connectionSocket.recv(1024)
    connectionSocket.send(modifiedMessage)
    connectionSocket.close()

# Client
clientSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)
clientSocket.connect((serverName, serverPort))
clientSocket.send(message)
modifiedMessage = clientSocket.recv(1024)
clientSocket.close()

Key points: - accept() creates new connection socket per client - Welcoming socket (listens) vs connection socket (data transfer) - Reliable, ordered byte stream - send()/recv() don't need address (connection-oriented)

items.title: 2.6.3 Socket Programming with QUIC
items.text:
• Uses libraries like aioquic (Python)
  • Similar to TCP but with streams, 0-RTT, connection migration
  • Application handles TLS certificates

items.title: Key Formulas (Chapter 2)
items.text:
Scenario Total Time Non-persistent (K objects) K × (2×RTT + L/R) Non-persistent (P parallel) ceil(K/P) × (2×RTT + L/R) Persistent (no pipelining) 2×RTT + K×L/R Persistent + Pipelining 2×RTT + K×L/R (requests back-to-back) HTTP/2 / HTTP/3 RTT_handshake + RTT_req/resp + L/R

DNS: 3-level lookup = 8 messages (4 queries + 4 replies) TTL: Typically 2 days = 172,800 seconds

items.title: Complete Questions, Examples, and MCQs from Slides and Textbook
Numerical Problems (Exam Practice)
items.text:
Q1. HTTP Performance Calculation: A web page consists of a base HTML (100 KB) + 5 embedded images (200 KB each). RTT = 80 ms. Transmission rates: server link = 100 Mbps, client link = 50 Mbps. Calculate total time for: - a) Non-persistent HTTP - b) Persistent HTTP (no pipelining) - c) Persistent HTTP (pipelining)

Answer: - a) 6 objects × (2 × 80 + 300KB/50Mbps) = 6 × (160 + 48) = 1248 ms - b) 2×80 + 6×(300KB/50Mbps) = 160 + 288 = 448 ms - c) 80 + 300KB/50Mbps + 80 + 5×300KB/50Mbps ≈ 240 ms

Q2. DNS Query Calculation: For a 3-level DNS lookup (root → TLD → authoritative), how many messages are exchanged? - Answer: 8 messages (4 queries + 4 replies)

Q3. DNS Caching: TTL = 2 days. How many seconds? - Answer: 172,800 seconds

items.text:

items.title: Unit 1: Computer Networks and the Internet + Application Layer
Overview
items.text:
This unit covers Chapters 1-2 of Kurose & Ross (9th Edition): - Chapter 1: Computer Networks and the Internet - Chapter 2: Application Layer

Course Hours: 14 hours

items.title: A Nuts-and-Bolts Description
items.text:
The Internet is a global network of networks - a complex infrastructure consisting of: - End systems (hosts): Computers, smartphones, servers, IoT devices (41+ billion IoT devices by 2027) - Communication links: Fiber optics, copper wire, coaxial cable, radio spectrum, satellite links - Packet switches: Routers and link-layer switches that forward packets - Protocols: TCP, IP, HTTP, DNS, etc. that control communication

Key concept: The Internet provides a service model to applications - a set of operations (send/receive) and expected behavior (reliability, timing, etc.)

items.title: A Services Description
items.text:
The Internet provides two key services to applications: 1. Connectionless service (UDP): Unreliable, no handshake, minimal overhead 2. Connection-oriented service (TCP): Reliable, in-order byte stream with flow/congestion control

Applications access these services via sockets - the API between application and transport layer.

items.title: What Is a Protocol?
items.text:
A protocol defines the format, order, and actions taken on transmission/receipt of messages among communicating entities. - Syntax: Message format, data representation - Semantics: Meaning of fields, actions to take - Timing: When to send, how fast, timeouts

Example: HTTP defines how a client requests a web page and how a server responds.

items.title: 1.2.1 Access Networks
items.text:
Access networks connect end systems to the first router (edge router). Types:

Access Network Technology Typical Speed Characteristics DSL Digital Subscriber Line ~24 Mbps downstream Uses existing telephone lines; dedicated per household Cable HFC (Hybrid Fiber-Coax) ~1-2 Gbps downstream Shared broadcast medium; uses DOCSIS FTTH Fiber to the Home ~1-10 Gbps Dedicated fiber; highest speeds 5G/Fixed Wireless Cellular ~100 Mbps - 1 Gbps Mobile/wireless; shared spectrum Enterprise (Ethernet/WiFi) 802.3/802.11 ~1-100 Gbps Wired/wireless LAN in organizations

Key distinction: - Dedicated access (DSL, FTTH): Bandwidth not shared - Shared access (Cable, WiFi, 5G): Bandwidth shared among users

items.title: 1.2.2 Physical Media
items.text: Medium Type Characteristics Twisted Pair (Cat 5e/6/6a/7) Copper 100m max; 1-10 Gbps; susceptible to interference Coaxial Cable Copper Longer distances; used in cable TV/HFC Fiber Optics (SMF/MMF) Glass Km distances; 10-100+ Gbps; immune to EMI Radio Spectrum Wireless WiFi, 4G/5G, satellite; shared medium; variable propagation

items.title: 1.3.1 Packet Switching
items.text:
The Internet uses packet switching (not circuit switching): - Messages broken into packets (typically 1-1500 bytes) - Each packet routed independently through network - Store-and-forward: Each switch receives entire packet before forwarding to next link - Statistical multiplexing: Links shared on demand; no reservation

Advantages over Circuit Switching: - Efficient for bursty data traffic - No connection setup delay - Better resource utilization - Robust (packets can take different paths)

items.title: 1.3.2 Circuit Switching (for comparison)
items.text:
• Dedicated end-to-end path reserved for duration of connection
  • Constant bandwidth guaranteed
  • Used in traditional telephone networks
  • Inefficient for bursty traffic (resources idle during silence)

items.title: 1.3.3 A Network of Networks
items.text:
The Internet = Interconnected ISPs: 1. Tier-1 ISPs: Global reach, peer with each other (no transit fees) 2. Tier-2 ISPs: Regional, buy transit from Tier-1 3. Tier-3/Access ISPs: Local, connect end users 4. Content Providers (CDNs): Google, Netflix, Akamai - deploy servers close to users 5. IXPs (Internet Exchange Points): Physical locations where ISPs peer

Peering vs Transit: - Peering: Mutual agreement, no payment (typically Tier-1 to Tier-1) - Transit: Customer pays provider for global connectivity

NIXI (National Internet Exchange of India): Nonprofit under MeitY, ~77 operational exchange nodes, handles >1.5 Tbps peak traffic. Keeps India-to-India traffic local.

items.title: 1.4 Delay, Loss, and Throughput in Packet-Switched Networks
1.4.1 Overview of Delay
items.text:
Total nodal delay at each router: 

d_nodal = d_proc + d_queue + d_trans + d_prop

Delay Component Formula Description Processing Delay (d_proc) ~microseconds Header check, routing table lookup, bit-error check Queuing Delay (d_queue) Variable Time waiting in output buffer; depends on traffic intensity Transmission Delay (d_trans) L / R Time to push packet bits onto link Propagation Delay (d_prop) d / s Time for bits to travel across link (speed of light ~2×10⁸ m/s in fiber)

Transmission Delay: d_trans = L / R - L = packet length (bits) - R = link bandwidth (bps)

Propagation Delay: d_prop = d / s - d = link length (meters) - s = propagation speed (m/s)

items.title: 1.4.2 Queuing Delay and Packet Loss
items.text:
Traffic Intensity: ρ = (L × a) / R = λL / R - a = average packet arrival rate (packets/sec) - λ = a (arrival rate) - ρ = fraction of time link is busy

Traffic Intensity Behavior ρ < 1 Stable, finite average queue ρ → 1 Queue grows, delay increases dramatically ρ > 1 Unstable, queue → ∞, packets dropped

Average Queuing Delay (M/M/1 queue): 

d_queue = (L/R) × (ρ / (1-ρ))

Packet Loss: Occurs when buffer is full. Lost packets may be retransmitted (TCP) or lost forever (UDP).

items.title: 1.4.3 End-to-End Delay
items.text:
For N links (no queuing/processing): 

d_end-end = N × (d_trans + d_prop)

General case: 

d_end-end = Σ(d_proc_i + d_queue_i + d_trans_i + d_prop_i)

items.title: 1.4.4 Throughput
items.text:
Instantaneous Throughput: Rate at which receiver gets bits Average Throughput: F / T (file size / transfer time)

Bottleneck Link: The link with minimum rate along path 

Throughput = min(R₁, R₂, ..., R_N)  (no cross traffic)

M flows sharing bottleneck R: 

Throughput_per_flow = R / M

items.title: 1.5 Protocol Layers and Their Service Models
1.5.1 Layered Architecture
items.text:
Five-Layer Internet Model: | Layer | Name | Key Protocols | Responsibility | |-------|------|---------------|----------------| | 5 | Application | HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP | Network applications | | 4 | Transport | TCP, UDP | Process-to-process delivery | | 3 | Network | IP, ICMP, routing protocols | Host-to-host delivery, routing | | 2 | Link | Ethernet, WiFi, PPP | Node-to-node delivery | | 1 | Physical | Cables, radio waves | Bit transmission |

OSI 7-Layer Model (for reference): 7. Application, 6. Presentation, 5. Session, 4. Transport, 3. Network, 2. Data Link, 1. Physical

items.title: 1.5.2 Encapsulation
items.text:
Each layer adds its own header (and sometimes trailer): 

Application Message
    → Transport Header + Message = Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP)
        → IP Header + Segment = Datagram
            → Link Header + Datagram + Link Trailer = Frame
                → Physical layer transmits bits

At receiver: Decapsulation - each layer strips its header and passes payload up.

items.title: 1.6 Networks Under Attack
items.text:
Types of attacks: 1. Malware: Viruses, worms, botnets, ransomware 2. DoS/DDoS: Overwhelm target with traffic 3. Sniffing/Eavesdropping: Passive interception 4. Spoofing: Fake source IP/email 5. Man-in-the-Middle: Intercept and modify 6. DNS Attacks: Cache poisoning, hijacking

Defense: Firewalls, IDS/IPS, encryption (TLS/IPsec), authentication, access control

items.title: 1.7 History of Computer Networking
items.text: Era Key Developments 1961-1972 Packet switching theory (Kleinrock, Baran, Davies); ARPANET (1969); NCP protocol 1972-1980 Email (Tomlinson); TCP/IP (Cerf & Kahn, 1974); Ethernet (Metcalfe, 1976) 1980-1990 TCP/IP standardized (1983); DNS (1984); NSFNET backbone; Routing protocols (RIP, OSPF, BGP) 1990s Web (Berners-Lee, 1990); Mosaic browser; Commercial ISPs; Dot-com boom 2000s-Present Broadband, WiFi, Mobile (3G/4G/5G), Cloud, CDNs, SDN, IoT, QUIC/HTTP/3

items.title: 2.1.1 Network Application Architectures
items.text:
Two main paradigms:

Architecture Description Examples Client-Server Always-on server (fixed IP) serves clients; clients don't communicate directly Web, Email, DNS Peer-to-Peer (P2P) No always-on server; peers act as both clients and servers; self-scaling BitTorrent, Bitcoin, Skype (original)

Hybrid: Many modern apps use both (e.g., P2P for content, centralized for discovery/auth).

items.title: 2.1.2 Processes Communicating
items.text:
• Process: Program running on end system
  • Client process: Initiates communication
  • Server process: Waits for contact
  • Socket: API between application and transport layer ("door")
  • Addressing: IP address + port number (16-bit)

Multiplexing/Demultiplexing: - Transport layer uses port numbers to deliver data to correct process - TCP: 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port) - UDP: 2-tuple (dst IP, dst port)

items.title: 2.1.3 Transport Services Available to Applications
items.text:
Service TCP UDP Reliable delivery ✓ ✗ In-order delivery ✓ ✗ Flow control ✓ ✗ Congestion control ✓ ✗ Connection setup 3-way handshake None Header overhead 20+ bytes 8 bytes

Neither TCP nor UDP provides: - Delay guarantees (max latency) - Bandwidth guarantees (min throughput)

items.title: 2.1.4 Application-Layer Protocols
items.text:
Define: - Message types (request/response) - Message syntax (fields, headers) - Field semantics (meaning) - Rules for when/how processes send/respond

Open protocols (standards): HTTP, SMTP, DNS - defined in RFCs Proprietary protocols: Skype (original), some gaming protocols

items.title: 2.2.1 Overview of HTTP
items.text:
• HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol): Web's application-layer protocol
  • Client: Browser (requests objects)
  • Server: Web server (responds with objects)
  • Objects: HTML, images, CSS, JS, videos - each addressable by URL
  • Stateless: Server maintains no client state between requests

URL format: http://host:port/path

items.title: 2.2.2 Non-Persistent vs Persistent Connections
items.text:
Connection Type Description RTTs for K objects Non-persistent (HTTP/1.0) New TCP connection per object K × 2 RTTs Persistent (HTTP/1.1) Single TCP connection for multiple objects 2 RTT + K×transmission Pipelined Persistent Send requests back-to-back without waiting 2 RTT + K×transmission

HTTP/1.0: Default non-persistent (can use Connection: keep-alive) HTTP/1.1: Default persistent, supports pipelining (rarely used due to head-of-line blocking)

items.title: 2.2.3 HTTP Message Format
items.text:
Request Message: 

GET /path/to/object HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Accept: text/html
Connection: keep-alive

[optional body for POST/PUT]

Response Message: 

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Mon, 03 Nov 2026 12:00:00 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 1234
Connection: keep-alive

<html>...</html>

Common Methods: GET, POST, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS Common Status Codes: - 200 OK, 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified - 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found - 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable

items.title: 2.2.4 Cookies
items.text:
Problem: HTTP is stateless; servers need to identify users across requests Solution: Cookies (RFC 6265)

How it works: 1. Server sends Set-Cookie: id=12345 in response header 2. Browser stores cookie locally 3. Browser includes Cookie: id=12345 in future requests to same domain 4. Server uses cookie to maintain session state

Components: Name, value, expiry, domain, path, Secure flag, HttpOnly flag

items.title: 2.2.5 Browser Caching
items.text: Goal: Reduce latency, bandwidth, server load Mechanism: - Server sends Cache-Control: max-age=3600 or Expires header - Browser caches response - On subsequent request: if fresh, use cached copy; if stale, conditional GET with If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match (ETag) - Server responds 304 Not Modified if unchanged

items.title: 2.2.6 HTTP/2 (RFC 7540)
items.text:
Improvements over HTTP/1.1: 1. Binary framing (not text) - more efficient parsing 2. Multiplexing - multiple streams over single TCP connection 3. Header compression (HPACK) - reduces overhead 4. Server push - server can send resources proactively 5. Stream prioritization - critical resources first

Problem: Head-of-line blocking still exists at TCP level (one lost packet blocks all streams)

items.title: 2.2.7 HTTP/3 and QUIC
items.text:
QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections): - Runs over UDP (not TCP) - Implements reliability, congestion control, TLS 1.3 in user space - 0-RTT resumption for repeat connections - Connection migration - survives IP change (mobile handoff) - Per-stream flow control - no head-of-line blocking across streams

HTTP/3 = HTTP semantics over QUIC - Same request/response model as HTTP/2 - But no TCP head-of-line blocking

items.title: 2.3.1 SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol)
items.text:
• Port 25 (server-to-server), Port 587 (client submission with TLS)
  • Push protocol: Sender pushes to receiver
  • Text-based commands: HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, QUIT
  • Reliable: Uses TCP
  • 7-bit ASCII only (requires MIME for binary/attachments)

Flow: 

Client → MTA (Mail Transfer Agent) → ... → MTA → Recipient's Mail Server

items.title: 2.3.2 Mail Message Formats
items.text:
RFC 5322 (message format): 

From: sender@example.com
To: recipient@example.com
Subject: Hello
Date: Mon, 03 Nov 2026 12:00:00 GMT
Message-ID: <unique@id>

Body text here...

MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) - RFC 2045: - Content-Type: text/plain, text/html, multipart/mixed, image/jpeg, etc. - Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64, quoted-printable, 7bit - Enables attachments, non-ASCII, multipart messages

items.title: 2.3.3 Mail Access Protocols
items.text:
Protocol Port Description POP3 110 (995 TLS) Download and delete; simple, offline access IMAP 143 (993 TLS) Remote folder management; sync across devices; server-side search HTTP 80/443 Webmail (Gmail, Outlook.com) - uses web API

SMTP = sending mail; POP3/IMAP = reading mail

items.title: 2.4.1 Services Provided by DNS
items.text:
1. Hostname to IP translation (primary)
  2. Host aliasing (CNAME records)
  3. Mail server aliasing (MX records)
  4. Load distribution (multiple A records for same name)
  5. Service discovery (SRV records)

items.title: 2.4.2 How DNS Works
items.text:
Hierarchical, distributed database: 

Root (.) → TLD (.com, .org, .edu) → Authoritative (example.com)

DNS Servers: 1. Root servers (13 logical, hundreds physical): Know TLD servers 2. TLD servers: Know authoritative servers for domains 3. Authoritative servers: Know actual records for domain 4. Local/Recursive resolvers: ISP/company DNS; perform recursive queries

Query Types: - Recursive: Resolver does all work, returns final answer - Iterative: Resolver asks root → TLD → authoritative step by step

Caching: All responses cached (TTL typically 2 days = 172,800 sec)

items.title: 2.4.3 DNS Records and Messages
items.text:
Resource Record Format: (Name, Value, Type, TTL)

Type Name Value Purpose A hostname IPv4 address Name → IPv4 AAAA hostname IPv6 address Name → IPv6 CNAME alias canonical name Alias → real name MX domain mail server hostname Mail routing NS domain authoritative NS Delegation TXT domain arbitrary text SPF, DKIM, verification SRV service host:port Service discovery

DNS Message Format: 

Header (12 bytes): ID, flags, QDCOUNT, ANCOUNT, NSCOUNT, ARCOUNT
Question Section: QNAME, QTYPE, QCLASS
Answer Section: RRs
Authority Section: RRs
Additional Section: RRs

Flags: QR (0=query, 1=response), Opcode, AA (authoritative), TC (truncated), RD (recursion desired), RA (recursion available), RCODE

items.title: 2.4.4 DNS Security
items.text:
• DNSSEC: Cryptographic signatures on records (RRSIG, DNSKEY, DS)
  • DoH/DoT: DNS over HTTPS/TLS for privacy
  • Attacks: Cache poisoning, DDoS on root/TLD, hijacking

items.title: 2.5 Video Streaming and Content Distribution Networks
2.5.1 Internet Video
items.text: Characteristics: High bandwidth, delay-tolerant (buffering), loss-tolerant Types: - Stored video: YouTube, Netflix (pre-recorded) - Live streaming: Twitch, sports (real-time encoding) - Interactive video: Zoom, FaceTime (low latency critical)

items.title: 2.5.2 HTTP Streaming and DASH
items.text:
Problem: Traditional streaming (RTSP/RTP) doesn't traverse firewalls well Solution: DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) - Video encoded at multiple bitrates/qualities - MPD (Media Presentation Description): XML manifest listing segments - Client adapts quality based on measured bandwidth - Segments fetched via standard HTTP GET

Quality adaptation algorithms: Buffer-based, throughput-based, hybrid

items.title: 2.5.3 Content Distribution Networks (CDNs)
items.text:
Problem: Single server far from users → high latency, low throughput CDN Solution: Deploy server clusters (PoPs) globally

CDN Operations: 1. Request routing: DNS redirects to nearest PoP (GeoDNS, anycast) 2. Content placement: Popular content cached at edge 3. Content delivery: Serve from cache or fetch from origin

Types: - Private CDNs: Netflix Open Connect, Google Global Cache - Third-party CDNs: Akamai, Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront

Benefits: Lower latency, higher throughput, reduced origin load, DDoS absorption

items.title: 2.6.1 Socket Programming with UDP
items.text:
UDP Socket API (Python): 

# Server
serverSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM)
serverSocket.bind(('', port))
while True:
    message, clientAddress = serverSocket.recvfrom(2048)
    serverSocket.sendto(modifiedMessage, clientAddress)

# Client
clientSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM)
clientSocket.sendto(message, (serverName, serverPort))
modifiedMessage, serverAddress = clientSocket.recvfrom(2048)

Key points: - sendto()/recvfrom() include destination address - No connection setup - Unreliable, unordered

items.title: 2.6.2 Socket Programming with TCP
items.text:
TCP Socket API (Python): 

# Server
serverSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)
serverSocket.bind(('', port))
serverSocket.listen(1)
while True:
    connectionSocket, addr = serverSocket.accept()
    message = connectionSocket.recv(1024)
    connectionSocket.send(modifiedMessage)
    connectionSocket.close()

# Client
clientSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)
clientSocket.connect((serverName, serverPort))
clientSocket.send(message)
modifiedMessage = clientSocket.recv(1024)
clientSocket.close()

Key points: - accept() creates new connection socket per client - Welcoming socket (listens) vs connection socket (data transfer) - Reliable, ordered byte stream - send()/recv() don't need address (connection-oriented)

items.text: Formula Equation Transmission Delay d_trans = L / R Propagation Delay d_prop = d / s Total Nodal Delay d_nodal = d_proc + d_queue + d_trans + d_prop End-to-End (N links, no queue/proc) d_end-end = N × (d_trans + d_prop) Traffic Intensity ρ = (L × a) / R Avg Queuing Delay (M/M/1) d_queue = (L/R) × (ρ / (1-ρ)) Store-and-Forward (1 packet, N links) d = N × L / R Store-and-Forward (P packets, N links) d = (N + P - 1) × L / R Bottleneck Throughput min(R₁, R₂, ..., R_N) M flows sharing bottleneck R / M

items.title: HTTP Performance
items.text:
Scenario Total Time Non-persistent (K objects) K × (2×RTT + L/R) Non-persistent (P parallel) ceil(K/P) × (2×RTT + L/R) Persistent (no pipelining) 2×RTT + K×L/R Persistent + Pipelining 2×RTT + K×L/R HTTP/2 / HTTP/3 RTT_handshake + RTT_req/resp + L/R

DNS: 3-level lookup = 8 messages (4 queries + 4 replies) TTL: Typically 2 days = 172,800 seconds

items.title: Review Questions
items.text:
1. Difference between packet switching and circuit switching?
  2. Packet: statistical multiplexing, store-and-forward, no reservation

  3. Circuit: dedicated path, guaranteed bandwidth, connection setup required

  4. What are the four delay components?

  5. Processing, Queuing, Transmission, Propagation

  6. When does packet loss occur?

  7. When router buffer is full (queue overflow)

  8. What determines end-to-end throughput?

  9. The bottleneck link (minimum rate along path)

  10. What is the difference between peering and transit?

  11. Peering: mutual, no payment; Transit: customer pays provider

  12. What is encapsulation?

  13. Each layer adds header/trailer to payload from layer above

  14. Client-server vs P2P?

  15. Client-server: dedicated always-on server

  16. P2P: peers act as both client/server, self-scaling

  17. What is a socket?

  18. API between application and transport layer; identified by (IP, port)

  19. TCP vs UDP services?

  20. TCP: reliable, ordered, flow/congestion control, connection-oriented

  21. UDP: unreliable, unordered, no flow/congestion control, connectionless

  22. Non-persistent vs persistent HTTP?

    • Non-persistent: new TCP per object (2 RTT each)
    • Persistent: single TCP for multiple objects

  23. How do cookies work?

    • Server sets cookie via Set-Cookie header
    • Browser sends cookie in future requests to same domain

  24. What is DNS and how does it work?

    • Hierarchical distributed database mapping names to IPs
    • Recursive/iterative queries; caching with TTL

  25. What is DASH?

    • HTTP-based adaptive streaming; client selects quality based on bandwidth

  26. What is a CDN?

    • Geographically distributed servers caching content near users

  27. UDP vs TCP socket programming?

    • UDP: sendto/recvfrom with address; no connection
    • TCP: connect/accept; send/recv without address; welcoming + connection sockets

items.title: Transport Services & UDP
items.text:
• Process-to-process delivery via ports (multiplexing/demultiplexing)
  • UDP: 2-tuple demux; TCP: 4-tuple demux
  • UDP header: src/dst port (16b), length (16b), checksum (16b) = 8 bytes
  • UDP checksum: 1's complement sum of 16-bit words + pseudo-header

items.title: Reliable Data Transfer (RDT)
items.text:
• RDT evolution: 1.0 (reliable) → 2.0 (bit errors, ACK/NAK) → 2.1 (corrupt ACK) → 2.2 (NAK-free) → 3.0 (loss + errors, timers)
  • Stop-and-wait utilization: U = (L/R) / (RTT + L/R)
  • Pipelining: sender allows multiple in-flight packets
  • GBN: cumulative ACK, window bound N ≤ 2ᵏ⁻¹, retransmit ALL on timeout
  • SR: selective ACK, per-packet timers, N ≤ 2ᵏ⁻¹, buffer out-of-order

items.title: TCP
items.text:
• Segment structure: seq# (byte of first data), ACK# (next expected byte), flags (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, PSH, URG, ECE, CWR), window (rwnd)
  • MSS = MTU - 40 (typically 1460 bytes)
  • RTT estimation: EstRTT = 0.875×EstRTT + 0.125×SampleRTT, DevRTT = 0.75×DevRTT + 0.25×|SampleRTT-EstRTT|
  • Timeout = EstRTT + 4×DevRTT, exponential backoff on timeout
  • Karn's Algorithm: don't measure SampleRTT for retransmitted segments
  • Sender: data from app → create segment, start timer if first; timeout → retransmit oldest, restart; ACK(y>SendBase) → SendBase=y, restart if unACKed remain
  • Fast retransmit: 3 dup ACKs → retransmit missing immediately, enter fast recovery
  • Fast recovery: ssthresh=cwnd/2, cwnd=ssthresh+3MSS, per dup ACK cwnd+=1MSS, on new ACK cwnd=ssthresh
  • Flow control: rwnd = RcvBuffer - (LastByteRcvd - LastByteRead), sender limits unACKed to min(cwnd, rwnd)
  • 3-way handshake: SYN(x) → SYN+ACK(y, x+1) → ACK(x+1, y+1)
  • 4-way teardown: FIN(u) → ACK(u+1) → FIN(v) → ACK(v+1), TIME_WAIT = 2×MSL

items.title: Congestion Control
items.text:
• Slow Start: cwnd=1 MSS (10 MSS per RFC 3390), per ACK cwnd+=1 MSS (doubles/RTT), exit when cwnd≥ssthresh
  • Congestion Avoidance: per RTT cwnd+=1 MSS (linear), per ACK cwnd+=MSS×(MSS/cwnd)
  • Timeout: ssthresh=cwnd/2, cwnd=1 MSS, enter Slow Start
  • 3 Dup ACKs: ssthresh=cwnd/2, cwnd=ssthresh+3 MSS, Fast Recovery
  • AIMD: Additive Increase (1 MSS/RTT), Multiplicative Decrease (÷2)
  • Macroscopic throughput: 0.75×W/RTT (W = cwnd at loss)
  • Loss rate model: Throughput ≈ 1.22×MSS/(RTT×√L)
  • CUBIC: cwnd = C×(t-K)³ + W_max, less RTT-dependent
  • Vegas: delay-based, Expected = cwnd/RTT_min, Actual = cwnd/RTT_curr
  • BBR: model-based, BDP = BW×RTT_min, pacing = BDP×gain, ignores loss
  • ECN: IP ECN bits (ECT0/ECT1/CE), TCP response: cwnd/=2, ssthresh=cwnd, set CWR

items.title: QUIC/HTTP/3
items.text:
• TCP+TLS 1.3 = 2 RTT; QUIC+TLS 1.3 = 1 RTT; QUIC 0-RTT resume
  • Connection ID survives IP change (migration)
  • Stream independence: lost packet blocks only that stream
